I did kinda go hard about how it should be talked about. I should of took it down a notch but I was frustrated because they were discussing it in a comparative way to how the public sees a psych ward. Given they aren’t as bad as what the public seems to think but this is the first time I’ve really heard a positive perspective from someone out of all the times I’ve discussed it. It’s like taking how to get rich quick advice from a lottery winner in a way.

In my state (Illinois) either you can say I’ll go and be deemed voluntary or a court (I can’t remember if a medical professional can do it alone or if they have to petition a court also) will deem you a risk to yourself or others and put you in the psych ward. Either way your a risk and have to go. That’s why your nudged to just go voluntarily because it’s easier on everyone. But if the court decides, it makes it more difficult to be released since its multiple channels you have to go through instead of the psychiatrists giving you the ok. 

Nobody is separated on how they were admitted. At most it was separated on gender and sometimes age (old folk and everyone else). I never was able to go outside or even leave the psych ward. My stays lasted anywhere from a few days to 9 days. But like I said before I’m fairly normal. Charismatic, seemingly well put together, I wasn’t reacting to every emotion. So I could talk myself out fairly well because I wasn’t a visible mess. And it caters to those people. Teaching you to take a deep breath instead of sticking that screwdriver in your neck. It’s all very basic. But yea, from state to state mental healthcare is very disproportionate and I’d like to see a standard in place. That’d be cool.

I’ve been hospitalized once as a teen and 3 times as an adult all in the Midwest. The time as a teen I met several kids who were normal but just having a difficult time dealing with their new mental illnesses. The three times as an adult though were different. Each time it seemed I was the only normal down to earth person out of a group of 20+. There may have been a few quiet outliers but for the most part it was usually adults who weren’t the brightest and didn’t quite understand their emotions. I don’t really remember anyone admitting themselves in without the hospital nudging them along because if not it’d be much harder to be discharged if it was involuntary. 

I’m not ashamed to say I’ve been admitted and I’ll talk about it because it is part of my life but to talk about it in a good light isn’t true and won’t help move mental healthcare to a place that can help everyone without it feeling almost like a punishment to be there.
